To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

transection of the chorda tymani and glossopharyngeals nerves, which innervate taste receptors on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and posterior one-third of the tongue, respectively, results in a 1.5-log unit increase in quinine detection thresholds.

the glossopharyngel and chorda tympanic nerves are not necessary for normal sensitivity in rats to low quinine concentration provided one of the nerves is intact; however, when both of these nerves are transected the remaining afferents input is not sufficient for maintaining normal detection performance.
the combined glossopharygeal and chorda tympaani nerves are necessary for normal detection of quinine in rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms that mediate the detection of bitter taste in the rat.
the effects of gustatory nerve lesions on taste function.
the role of the glossopharygeal and chorda tympans nerve in the detection of bitter taste.
